syllabus.clause: the engine plans one incremental batch per trigger against new source offsets; offset log (write-ahead) and commit log in the checkpoint; trigger types (processingTime, availableNow; once deprecated); why micro-batch latency floors sit around hundreds of milliseconds.

items.item: markMicroBatchEnd commits the offset to the commit log only after the microbatch has completed execution

at.step: Elaborate: a log that's replayed, never guessed

items.item: The offset log and commit log together let Spark classify a failed run precisely on restart: a batch with an offset-log entry but no matching commit-log entry is known to be incomplete and must be rerun from that exact offset, never silently skipped or silently re-read from scratch.

at.out: the precise failure classification the two-log design enables named only; this topic's own examples.py confirms the logs exist and stay in lockstep, not the restart-time branch logic that reads them

items.item: Continuous processing mode (experimental, mentioned only in passing in CHAPTER.md's own handoff) abandons the micro-batch model entirely for a long-running task per partition, trading the checkpoint-based fault tolerance this topic measures for true low, sub-millisecond latency and a narrower set of supported operations (no aggregations).

at.out: continuous processing's own tradeoff against micro-batch named only, as the structurally different model this topic's own handoff gestures toward; this topic's own examples.py measures only micro-batch triggers

items.item: spark.sql.streaming.minBatchesToRetain controls how many completed batches' worth of offset-log, commit-log, and state-store checkpoint data Spark keeps around rather than cleaning up -- a real, bounded cost of the write-ahead design this topic's own examples.py doesn't exercise (every probe query ran for only a handful of batches).

at.out: checkpoint retention and its own bounded storage cost named only; this topic's own examples.py never runs long enough to trigger cleanup

items.item: RocksDB state store changelog checkpointing (an alternative to the traditional snapshot-based checkpointing this topic's offset/commit logs sit alongside) uploads only the changes made to state since the last checkpoint rather than a full snapshot, reducing per-batch checkpoint cost specifically for stateful queries with large state -- a refinement to the checkpoint mechanism this topic's own stateless rate-source probes never touch.

at.out: RocksDB changelog checkpointing named only as a refinement for stateful queries; this topic's own examples.py uses no stateful operators and so never checkpoints state

items.item: The availableNow trigger's own fallback behavior -- performing a one-time micro-batch instead when any source doesn't support Trigger.AvailableNow -- means a query author can't always assume the stronger guarantee just by requesting it; the actual trigger behavior depends on every source involved, not just the one requested.

at.out: the availableNow-to-one-time fallback and its source-dependence named only; this topic's own examples.py uses the rate source, which supports availableNow, so the fallback path never triggers

items.item: queryPlanning time, one of the named components inside a batch's own durationMs breakdown (alongside getBatch, addBatch, commitOffsets, and walCommit), is itself a measurable sub-cost of the latency floor this topic names only in aggregate -- re-optimizing the identical incremental plan every single trigger is part of what the floor actually pays for.

at.out: queryPlanning as a specific, measurable component of the aggregate latency floor named only; this topic's own examples.py asserts the aggregate triggerExecution floor, not the queryPlanning sub-component specifically

items.item: A rate source's own deterministic row generation (each partition produces a fixed, predictable sequence keyed by elapsed time) makes it a reliable tool for probing trigger timing precisely, unlike a file or Kafka source, where variable data arrival would confound a latency-floor or trigger-spacing measurement with genuine data-volume variance.

at.out: why the rate source specifically suits a timing probe named only; this topic's own examples.py uses the rate source for exactly this reason, without stating the reasoning inline

items.item: Kafka's own offset semantics (a monotonically increasing per-partition integer) versus the file source's own offset representation (a set of file names already processed) show the offset log's abstraction holding across genuinely different underlying mechanisms -- this topic's own examples.py measures the rate source's own simple numeric offset, one instance of a general mechanism.

at.out: offset representation varying by source, with the offset log abstracting over all of them, named only; this topic's own examples.py uses only the rate source's own offset format

items.item: spark.sql.streaming.noDataMicroBatches.enabled governs whether a trigger still runs a micro-batch when no new data has arrived -- relevant specifically to advancing the watermark and clearing old state on a schedule, a case this topic's own examples.py never exercises since its probes always have data flowing from the rate source.

at.out: no-data micro-batches and their own watermark-advancement purpose named only; this topic's own examples.py always has new data available, so a no-data batch never runs

items.item: walCommit, a separate named component in a batch's own durationMs breakdown from commitOffsets, is specifically the cost of durably writing the write-ahead log entry itself to the checkpoint's storage backend -- distinguishing the cost of the write-ahead mechanism's own durability from the cost of deciding what to write.

at.out: walCommit as its own distinct cost component, separate from commitOffsets, named only; this topic's own examples.py reads the aggregate triggerExecution time, not this specific sub-component
